articles.title: Message from Nepal
articles.content: THREE features of thecatastrophic floodthat tore through Nepal on Aug 16, 2026, do not fit Pakistan’s mountain disaster strategy: it started without rains; it originated across the border; it had huge compounding factors. None of these three is a one-off. They describe a disaster category that has been forming across the region for over a decade, growing more frequent, widespread and severe. But Pakistan’s climate planning has stayed focused almost entirely on the monsoon. A mass of rock and glacier ice broke away from an altitude of about 5,200 metres in the upper mountain range, generating seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake. The fall produced enough friction to melt the ice on the way down, turning a dry avalanche into a slurry of mud, ice and boulders moving at up to 167 kilometres an hour at a height of 9m. The debris choked the river and formed a dam. When that gave way, a second surge followed; both hit settlements and the hydropower works below. It started above the cloud levels. Slopes at this altitude are held up by permafrost gluing the rock and glacial ice buttressing the valley walls. Warming removes both: thawing permafrost raises pore pressure and cuts shear strength, while retreating glaciers stop bracing the slopes from outside. The rock fails on temperature’s schedule, not the monsoon’s, which is why Chamoli in Uttarakhand in India went down under clear skies in 2021 and Langtang followed five years later. The record before both confirms a trend, not two isolated events. The 2015 avalanche off Langtang Lirung, the 2016 Gongbatongsha outburst crossing from the Tibet area into Nepal, and the 2024 Thame outburst in the Everest region struck without warning, each widening the geography of a hazard. High-altitude disasters underscore the need for Pakistan to go beyond monsoon planning. In Pakistan, the2010 Attabad collapsedammed the Hunza River and submerged 24 kilometres of the Karakoram Highway. The Shisper Glacier’s ice-dammed lakebreachedwithout rain in 2022 and destroyed the highway bridge at Hassanabad. Each event has moved higher in elevation, wider in geography, and heavier in what it destroys, from one buried village in 2015 to a cascading event spread over several kilometres. Pakistan keeps no comparable dataset on its own landslide activity. But a study in the National Science Review, covering more than 8,000 landslides across the eastern Himalayas, found a five-fold increase in high-elevation slope failures over three decades, tracking a doubling of Hindu Kush Himalaya glacier mass loss since 2000. Failures are also rising and entering the 5,000m-6,000m band that was once too frozen to fail. The Langtang collapse struck Gyirong Port, before the debris continued into Nepal’s own river systems. The direction of travel is not new. Nearly half of the more than 25 major glacial lake outburst floods recorded in Nepal since the mid-20th century have originated across the same border, arriving from a stretch neither country monitors jointly. This event was not itself a Glof — no lake burst before the collapse — but the debris dam it left behind and the discharge that followed sit inside the same unmonitored corridor. Pakistan belongs to the same geography, through the Kyagar Glacier’s periodic surges in the Shaksgam Valley. But China is not just Nepal’s or Pakistan’s upstream neighbour. It is South Asia’s upper riparian. It is the source plateau for the Indus, the Sutlej and the Brahmaputra — the headwaters of most of South Asia’s major rivers. That makes bilateral arrangements structurally insufficient. What this event calls for is a South Asia-wide early warning architecture, built and shared across every state whose rivers begin on that plateau, not a patchwork of separate deals each covering one border and missing the rest. None of Nepal’s responses fixed the underlying failure. Built for a slow monsoon rise, its flood sensors were destroyed before they could warn of a moving slurry. Existing bilateral arrangements track slow glacial lake outbursts, not sudden ice-rock collapse. Nepal had no real-time alert before the surge. Pakistan, sharing the same upstream geography, has the identical gap. What Pakistan needs:Dasu, Diamer-Bhasha and Mohmand are located in river corridors engineered for a monsoon flood profile, not the debris slurry that trapped 500 workers in Nepal. The Karakoram Highway has already been severed once at Attabad and once at Hassanabad. A third closure is not hypothetical. Nepal rewrote its school-siting rules before rebuilding, not after. It accepted specialised help without inviting chaos. Pakistan’s community-based disaster risk management networks in Gilgit-Baltistan and KP already have the local trust that saved lives on the Trishuli corridor before state machinery arrived. What they lack is a local government signal to act on before the water reaches them. Four steps are needed. First, convert the existing weather arrangement with China into automated, real-time information sharing on slope deformation and barrier-lake formation in the Shaksgam and Xinjiang zones — the exact category the Nepal-China arrangement missed. Second, focus on joint satellite monitoring with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, ICIMOD and Suparco, using synthetic aperture radars across the Karakoram, Pamirs and Hindu Kush structured from the outset as a Saarc-wide facility that India, Bhutan and Bangladesh can draw on since all sit downstream of the same plateau. Third, install seismic and hydrological sensors along the Indus and Shyok corridors calibrated for a slurry, not a rising river, so that downstream infrastructure gets lead time measured in hours instead of minutes. Fourth, join the consortium undertaking primary technical monitoring, satellite radar analysis, and field assessments, led by ICIMOD, the United States Geological Survey, Integrated Research on Disaster Risk, Nepal Environment Society, and academic glaciologists from such institutions as the University of Michigan. They are combining real-time remote-sensing satellite tracking with ground-level hydrological stations. These entities are quantifying the initial collapse volume, utilising synthetic aperture radar to monitor adjacent unstable slopes, assessing secondary barrier-lake outburst risks, and advancing regional hazard-mapping protocols — areas of critical importance to Pakistan. This catastrophe combines rapid- and slow-onset — the compound hazard now falling inside the mandate of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage. The writer serves on the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.
articles.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh

articles.title: The confidence game
articles.content: NOTHING gives them confidence like a pile of dollars in the reserves. Over the decades, I have seen this trend. Whoever is ruling Pakistan lacks confidence in themselves while the foreign exchange reserves are low and large debt-service payments are looming on the horizon. But the situation always turns, like these things do. After a few years of a gruelling, IMF-mandated adjustment, the reserves are rebuilt; import cover and debt service cover both rise, and with them also the confidence of the ruler. It is happening one more time. The foreign exchange reserves have been rebuilt since July 2023. Both reserve adequacy ratios — import and debt service cover — show notable improvements since their low points between the summer of 2022 and 2023. The reserves were barely able to cover 13 per cent of scheduled maturities in the year ahead and three weeks of imports at the low point of both these ratios in December 2022. From there, they have risen and today can cover almost 70pc of scheduled maturities over the next 12 months and more than three months of imports. The rulers have gained confidence alongside this development, to the point where they feel they are now in a position to dictate terms to their partners in government and seek a major and far-reachingchange in the structure of the federation. It almost seems like they took the critique that they had failed to bring about structural reforms to heart. But in seeking to change the very structure of the state, over the objections of the parties whose support helped usher in their government, they might be acting out of a sense of overconfidence. The improvement in the reserve adequacy ratios is real, but it is already showing signs of having peaked. Consider just what the last seven months have seen. Reserves rose during this period, but the pace of the rise decelerated. Average 12-month reserve increases remained at a high of $5.7 billion till May, then fell to $3.9bn in June and then to $2.7bn in July. More importantly, the rising reserves procured diminishing adequacy when measured against rising import requirements. Despite a billion-dollar increase in liquid reserves between January and July, import cover barely moved past 3.1 months. Once the trajectory peaks and the reserve decline kicks in, confidence drains out of the government. This is usually how it begins. It is not clear yet whether therecent $3bn raised via the Eurobond auctionwill actually stay in the country or be used to retire bilateral debt, as some of the reporting suggests. If the latter, then it will help raise the debt-service coverage ratio but will place more pressure on import cover. These are signs that on the present trajectory, the reserve accumulation that began in July 2023 has peaked. Once the incremental reserves procure diminishing increases in the twin coverage ratios, and trade-offs begin appearing between improvements in debt-service coverage and import cover, it can be said that the organic trajectory driving reserve accumulation has hit its built-in limit. From here on, either the trade-offs will sharpen, leading to a peak in reserves followed by a decline, or the government will find alternative sources to continue the build-up. The alternative sources could be Exim Bank financing of some sort from the US, coupled with aline from the US Treasury, assuming it comes through. It could also be more favourable rollovers of existing bilateral maturities, something we will see by December when the Saudi deposits mature. But one thing is certain. Once the trajectory peaks and the reserve decline kicks in, confidence drains out of the government. The window in which to do dramatic things closes, the resource envelope shrinks and the government goes into defensive mode. That time may still be a little while away. But given how the reserve metrics are shaping up, it would seem that either the rulers have some large-scale inflows lined up or they have come a little late to the game of rearranging the deckchairs. The situation is aggravated by high oil prices, brought on by the prolonged stand-off that the war in the Middle East has devolved into. With oilalready touching $100, global oil inventories depleted and the Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb straits both under fire, the outlook for oil prices is anything but sunny. Given high oil prices and the great difficulty they are having in procuring LNG cargoes, the real impact of energy prices is yet to land. The external sector has improved over the past few years — there is no doubt about that. But three things need to be underlined again and again. First, the improvement is not on the scale needed to support a revival of growth, because the burn rates of the reserves that come with growth rates of 6pc or more in Pakistan mean these reserves will barely last 12 months. Second, the improvement is hitting a plateau and will need a fresh line of inflows to sustain itself in the months ahead. And third, a high-energy-price scenario is rapidly taking shape before us; this might be prolonged, which could aggravate the fragility of the external sector in Pakistan. This is not the time for adventurism or for opening up unnecessary fronts domestically. Going forward, the government is likely to see a rising arc of pressure spreading across the horizon from multiple directions. At a time like this, it needs its decision-making system at home to be on an even keel. This is a bad time to be an embattled ruler, especially if that is a choice that can be avoided. All rulers in the past 25 years have succumbed to the overconfidence that comes with a healing external sector and rising foreign exchange reserves. It’s almost funny how that works: the confidence game in Pakistan is so closely tied to the quantity of dollars in its treasury. But it’s a good idea not to over-count those dollars just yet. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: See for yourself
articles.content: MAN proposes, God disposes. If Prometheus was punished by the gods for stealing fire, modern man is being punished by nature for harnessing free-flowing water behind dams. Dams were invented when agro-based human communities needed to store water for seasonal irrigation. The earliest known dam is the Jawa Dam in Jordan, dateable to about 3,000 BCE. The ancient Egyptians, the Romans, the early Indians, and the Chinese imperial dynasties built dams to ensure fertility. Europe woke up late. In the 12th century, the Dutch dammed the river Amstel. They gave the word ‘dam’ permanence by including it in the names of their cities: Amsterdam, Rotterdam. The Industrial Revolution in the 19th century and the spread of British influence saw the development of dams in Canada, India, Australia, and Egypt. The first Aswan Dam (in its day, the largest masonry dam) was built by a British firm and financed by Ernest Cassel (better known today as the grandfather of Lady Edwina Mountbatten). Completed in 1902, it remained an engineering marvel until superseded by the present Aswan Dam, completed in the 1970s. The project became a pawn in superpower politics. Offers of financing by the US and Britain were withdrawn after they were angered by Nasser’s recognition of communist China. It was completed with Russian aid. In the 1930s, the US government, to alleviate the social impact of the Great Depression, ordered the construction of the Hoover Dam across the Colorado River. Despite its challenging complexity, the Six Companies consortium completed the dam, two years ahead of schedule. Nature has reminded mankind of its lethal power. In the 1960s, because of the heavy outlay in large dam projects, the World Bank assumed the burden borne by governments. It funded large dams in Latin America, Africa and Asia. After a lull in the 1990s, triggered by ecological concerns, silting, and population displacement, it has resumed its support, funding projects in Tajikistan, Bhutan and Pakistan. Pakistan has depended heavily on the World Bank to finance major dam projects — Tarbela, Mangla, and most recently the Dasu Hydropower Project, to which it has committed $2.3 billion. Pakistan became independent in 1947 and China in 1949. Since then, Pakistan has built over 1,000 reservoirs and dams. It has about 150 larger dams (over 15 metres tall). China has built 98,000 dams, including the massive 22,500 MW Three Gorges Dam (TGD) on the Yangtze River. (Tarbela’s capacity is around 5,000 MW.) Structurally, they differ. The TGD is a concrete gravity dam. Tarbela is an earth-filled dam, and therein lies its geophysical vulnerability. On Aug 22, 1976, Tarbela, still under construction, developed a fault, serious enough for prime minister Z.A. Bhutto to air-dash to the site. US ambassador Henry Byroade reported to Washington that the emergency resulted from the failure of Tunnel 2. A decision was taken to open Tunnel 1 and to drain the lake (over 20 days) so that the tunnels could be inspected. Separately, Tunnels 3 and 4 had to be closed down due to “severe concrete erosion”. Panic set in as people feared that the sudden release of water from Tarbela would destroy everything downstream, to Karachi. It did not help matters when the press reported that an American project engineer W. Shapiro had committed suicide, leaving a note “disclosing an error in design”. Fifty years later, nature has reminded mankind of its lethal power. On Aug 26, 2026, a catastrophe occurred on the Nepal-China border when a melting glacier collapsed in the Himalayas, precipitating an avalanche of water, rock and soil into the Trishuli River valley. The debris flow swept away everything in its path, breaking down dams, bridges and human settlements. More than 1,000 people have died. Over 4,500 are missing. One is reminded of the manmade havoc caused during World War II, when on the night of May 16-17, 1943, the RAF destroyed three German dams, flooding Germany’s industrial Ruhr valley. The RAF used “bouncing bombs” that could skip across water (like pebbles) and then explode near the dam. “The resulting floods destroyed power stations, factories, mines, and downstream bridges, severely impacting German war production.” That British tactic should be a warning to combatant nations locked in water wars. Water flow may be used as a weapon, but water dammed is especially vulnerable. No country has so far used nuclear weapons, nor dams as targets. That will not prevent some deranged Dr Strangelove from pressing the doomsday button. Twenty years ago, Al Gore warned of the impact of climate change and global warming in a documentary An Inconvenient Truth. The critic, who dismissed that documentary as “a blatant intellectual fraud”, should now be invited to help those searching for the dead in the Trishuli River valley.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Why only JI?
articles.content: PARLIAMENTARY debate, judicial forums, and institutional safety valves often fail to rescue the public when elite capture is deeply entrenched and the cost of living becomes unbearable. Fresh elections may not offer much hope either, as the electoral process is widely perceived to be managed to favour a chosen flock. Under such conditions, public protest becomes an appealing instrument for citizens in distress. Across the world, there are many examples where mass protests have achieved their objectives while remaining peaceful. Pakistan, however, presents a troubling dilemma. Its economic and governance problems are severe. Household incomes are under intense pressure from high electricity bills and an unjustified petroleum levy. The government continues to overtax the salaried class and formal businesses instead of reducing its own operating expenses. Such conditions usually trigger widespread public unrest. Yet the streets of Pakistan, particularly in Sindh and Punjab, remain largely calm. Political parties are unwilling to mobilise people over agonising economic concerns, with the exception of Jamaat-i-Islami. While the silence on the part of mainstream parties is quite understandable, JI presents an interesting case study. The PPP, PML-N, and MQM are part of the ruling coalition and are enjoying the perks of power. A party sitting in a government that implements painful economic policies cannot credibly stage a sit-in against that same system. The PTI’s absence is more tragic. In the past, the party led large protest movements. For now, even as it embarks on another drive for its founder’s release, it is effectively without a central leadership, and its decision-making structure is fragmented. Its current incapacity is therefore better explained by state pressure and a leadership crisis than by indifference to economic issues. JI’s strength comes from organisation rather than the ballot box. JI, on the other hand, is active on the streets though virtually absent from parliament. While JI has consistently failed in Pakistan’s electoral arithmetic, its street mobilisation has contributed to policy changes on several occasions. In fact, JI has never primarily been a vote-thirsty party. Its strength has traditionally come from organisation rather than the ballot box. It possesses a disciplined body of workers, a student wing, a women’s wing, and an extensive welfare network, which together give it a strong followers’ base. It therefore plays to its strength. This is perhaps one of the key factors that explain its continued presence on the streets. JI’s periodic public campaigns allow it to keep its followers engaged and available. Its organisational capacity is a standing political asset that might otherwise remain underused. Interestingly, other political parties lack sufficient motivation to stay continuously engaged with their followers. For example, the PPP and PML-N rely heavily on electables and influential families rather than on grassroots workers. JUI-F has a captive audience in its madressah network, which can be mobilised whenever needed. JI does not possess such advantages. Its support base is principally shaped by the ideology of Maulana Maududi. Even a powerful ideology requires rituals to remain alive. JI’s protests and dharnas may therefore function as planned rituals to sustain its organisational life-force. Second, protests give JI something that elections have repeatedly denied it: visibility. Even when a protest does not immediately alter government policy, it places the party at the centre of the national debate. Major parties, associated with elite political families along with est-ablished vote banks, have unparalleled access to state institutions and media platforms. JI cannot compete with them through these channels; it seeks political relevance and visibility by taking ownership of issues that directly affect ordinary citizens. Third, there is nothing at stake politically for JI under the current governance structure. Free from the compromises of incumbency, JI can occupy the principled opposition space. By leading protests against inflation and the petroleum levy, JI can present itself as the only party addressing common despondencies. This positioning may earn it sympathy beyond its traditional support base. Finally, there is a moral dimension to JI’s activism. The party frames politics as a form of public responsibility rather than merely a contest for government offices. Its supporters expect it to speak out against injustice even when the likelihood of immediate electoral gains is limited. While JI must reassure the youth, women, minorities, and other segments of society regarding its ideological image, it would be a missed opportunity if its campaign against extractive public policies fails to attract their support.
articles.author: Farooq Arby

articles.title: Following through
articles.content: ECONOMIC policymaking requires private-sector buy-in to succeed. Yet our policymakers have rarely sought it without political prodding from the top. Even when they do, their instinct is to bury, ignore or delay implementing the recommendations. That is precisely why the prime minister deserves credit formaintaining periodic contact with the business community. But such interactions should deliver results, not merely generate positive headlines. Still, progress is visible, though the pace remains slow. Thesuper tax has been withdrawn, and some business costs have eased. The government also cites Rs800bn recovered through stronger enforcement over the past year without imposing new taxes on compliant businesses. That is a meaningful gain, but sustaining it demands deeper institutional reform. The PM’s view that growth must become export-led is correct. Pakistan’s domestic-demand-driven expansions follow a familiar pattern: they last for a while but then create external imbalances and return the country to stabilisation programmes. But intent is not enough. Predictable policies, competitively priced energy, long-term financing, reliable logistics and a regulatory environment that does not punish investment are needed. Currently, long-term investment is scarce and competitiveness continues to erode. Businessmen have pointed this out to the PM and his economic team several times during consultations. The PM and his team agree, but there is no follow-through. There is no record of which commitments from previous meetings were fulfilled. That pattern is why business confidence in these consultations continues to diminish even as the meetings go on. The meetings have value in principle. They bring to the government’s attention the obstacles businesses actually face and can build confidence in the process. In practice, however, they tend to become crowded affairs where a long list of grievances is aired without clear priorities or a mechanism to track what happens next. That must change. Future sessions should focus on specific reforms, with each action assigned to a ministry, given a deadline and measurable target, and made the responsibility of an identifiable official. The Prime Minister’s Office should directly oversee this process. A directive issued in a meeting room is not policy until it is recorded, assigned and pursued to completion. Too much of what is said in these forums disappears once the meeting ends. Public promises and announcements have never been in short supply — from this government or its predecessors. What has been missing is a clear and stable policy regime that allows businesses to plan and invest for the long term. Whether these consultations change that is the only test that matters. The dialogue channel the PM has established is worth keeping open. But its purpose must now shift from reassurance and the resolution of individual grievances to reforms that change the operating environment itself.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Loose talk
articles.content: OVER the weekend, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz made a statement at a public event that caused quite a stir. Striking a parochial note unbecoming of a public representative, the CM remarked that the threat to Punjab is “less from neighbouring countries and more from my neighbouring provinces”. For a political leader to take such an exclusivist position — one that sits uneasily alongside any aspiration to national leadership — is ill-advised. Referring to the bordering provinces, the CM said: “Terrorism enters Punjab from there. Everyone has their eyes on Punjab, but, thank God, Punjab remains safe. The kind of threats we face come from all our provincial borders.” She appeared to be contrasting her province’s ‘better management’ of law and order, militancy and related challenges with the crises other provinces continue to face. The Punjab information minister later sought to clarify that the CM was merely referring to the movement of terrorists across borders and never intended to target any ethnic community or province. Still, several political leaders took exception to the insinuation that terrorism is not Punjab’s problem but one for the other provinces to deal with. Opposition parties denounced the remarks as insulting, divisive and damaging to national unity. Many saw them as portraying KP and Balochistan as sources of terrorism rather than as long-suffering victims of it. That anger should be acknowledged. Both provinces have borne the brunt of terrorism, making countless sacrifices for decades. It is irresponsible to suggest, no matter how obliquely, that the pain they have suffered is theirs alone to bear. Terrorism and militancy represent a breakdown of the social contract — one that is simply more visible on the peripheries than in the heartland. Just because the heartland is comparatively stable does not mean it has no responsibility towards the rest of the federation. There is no place for casual provincialism in a society as heterogeneous as Pakistan. Leaders who ‘other-ise’ their opponents to capitalise on social prejudices are sowing the seeds for even greater instability. They believe this will solidify their legitimacy in the eyes of their constituents and consequently strengthen their hold on power. Instead, it will fracture society further and make it much more ungovernable. There is a reason the Quaid laid so much stress on unity. That emphasis must be reflected on.
articles.author: Editorial
